read.sections.0.heading.source: AI runs in big buildings full of chips
read.sections.0.heading.back: AI runs in big buildings full of chips

read.sections.0.text.source: When you ask an AI tool a question, your device usually doesn't make the answer itself. Some small tools can. But most of the time, the question travels to a data centre, a large building full of computers. Inside are thousands of chips that do trillions of sums every second. They use a lot of electricity and get very hot, so many data centres use water to cool them. An international energy agency estimated that in 2024, all the world's data centres used about 1.5% of its electricity. Only part of that was for AI. Data centres also run websites, videos and messages. The agency expects data centres to use about twice as much by 2030, mostly because of AI. That is a forecast, not a measurement.
read.sections.0.text.back: When you ask an AI tool a question, usually your device does not make the answer itself. Some small tools can. But almost always, that question is sent to a data centre, a big building full of computers. Inside are thousands of chips that do trillions of calculations every second. Those chips use a lot of electricity and become very hot, so many data centres use water to cool them. An international energy agency estimated that in 2024, all the data centres in the world used about 1.5% of the world's electricity. Only part of that amount was for AI. Data centres also run websites, videos and messages. That agency expects data centres to use about twice as much by 2030, mainly because of AI. That is an estimate, not a measurement.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Most of the time" as "hampir selalu" (almost always), a little stronger; "sering kali" (often) is weaker. Reviewers: choose. "Forecast" and "estimated" are both "perkiraan/memperkirakan" in Indonesian; the point that it is not a measurement is kept.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Usually, an AI answer is not made in your device. Some small tools do work on a phone. But most questions go to a data centre, a big building full of computers. Its chips do huge amounts of maths. They use a lot of power and get very hot. Water often helps to cool them. In 2024, all data centres used about 1.5% of the world's power. Only part was for AI. Experts think this may double by 2030, mostly because of AI. That is a forecast.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Usually, an AI answer is not made in your phone or laptop. Some small tools do work on a phone. But most questions are sent to a data centre, a big building full of computers. Its chips do very many calculations. Those chips use a lot of electricity and become very hot. Water is often used so the chips stay cool. In 2024, all data centres used about 1.5% of the world's electricity. Only part was for AI. Experts expect this amount may double by 2030, mainly because of AI. That is an estimate.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Chips need minerals and a few factories
read.sections.1.heading.back: Chips need minerals and a handful of factories

read.sections.1.text.source: Chips are made from materials dug out of the ground. Some need rare minerals, which are often mined in ways that harm nature. Very few factories can make the most powerful chips. In 2021, a chip industry study found that most of the world's most advanced chips were made in one place, Taiwan. So a problem in one place could cause chip shortages around the world. Old chips and computers also become electronic waste. This waste can contain harmful metals, such as mercury and lead.
read.sections.1.text.back: Chips are made from materials dug from the ground. Some need rare minerals, which are often mined in ways that damage nature. read.sections.1.text.note: "Most powerful" as "paling canggih" (most advanced), as Indonesian says of chips.

read.sections.1.simpler.back: Chips are made from things dug from the ground. Some need rare minerals. Digging them can damage nature. Only a few factories make the best chips. read.sections.2.text.source: Data centres are being built fast in Southeast Asia. Singapore paused new ones in 2019, and in 2021 they used about 7% of its electricity. Many companies then built in Johor, in Malaysia, and on Batam, in Indonesia. Data centres bring investment, building work that ends when the building is finished, and some long-term jobs. Malaysia's government hopes they will help to modernise its economy. But critics say they create far fewer jobs than they promise. Many of their users live in other countries. Some people nearby worry about water shortages and power cuts. Companies can lower these costs with more efficient AI, power from the sun and wind, and cleaned, reused water.
read.sections.2.text.back: Data centres are being built fast in Southeast Asia. Singapore temporarily stopped the building of new data centres in 2019, and in 2021 data centres used about 7% of Singapore's electricity. After that, many companies built in Johor, Malaysia, and on Batam Island, Indonesia. Data centres bring investment, building work that ends when the building is finished, and some long-term jobs. Malaysia's government hopes data centres will help modernise its economy. But critics say data centres create far fewer jobs than promised. Many of their users live in other countries. Some people who live nearby worry about water shortages and power cuts. Companies can lower these costs with more efficient AI, electricity from the sun and wind, and water that is cleaned and reused.
read.sections.2.text.note: Batam is in Indonesia, so Indonesian learners may know it well; the sensitive note asks teachers to keep this neutral.

watch.summary.source: Since 2019, more than a thousand huge AI data centres have been built around the world. Each one can use as much water as a small town. It can use as much electricity as a small city. Inside, there are thousands of racks of computers with special chips. These chips do trillions of sums every second, to answer questions and to train AI. All this work makes the chips very hot. Engineers cool them with water towers, cold water in pipes, or special liquids. They also send data with light instead of copper wires, which wastes less power. But AI tools keep getting bigger, so they need more and more electricity. The video asks if we could build smaller tools for smaller jobs. It ends with a question: how much of the planet's resources should we use for smarter machines?
watch.summary.back: Since 2019, more than a thousand very big AI data centres have been built around the world. Each data centre can use as much water as a small town. That data centre can use as much electricity as a small city. Inside, there are thousands of racks of computers with special chips. These chips do trillions of calculations every second, to answer questions and train AI. All this work makes the chips very hot. Engineers cool them with water towers, cold water in pipes, or special liquids. They also send data with light, not with copper cables, so less electricity is wasted. But AI tools keep becoming bigger, so those tools need more and more electricity. The video asks whether we could make smaller tools for smaller jobs. The video ends with a question: how many of the planet's resources should we use for smarter machines?
watch.summary.note: "Smarter machines" as "mesin yang lebih pintar"; "resources" as "sumber daya" (KEY_TERMS).

Electricity: the International Energy Agency's Energy and AI report (April 2025), as reported by Scientific American and Nature, estimated that all data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024, about 1.5% of the world's electricity, and projected about 945 TWh by 2030, roughly what Japan uses in a year now. The 1.5% is for all data centres, not AI alone: the IEA estimated that AI servers were about 15% of data-centre energy use in 2024, and one outside researcher thinks that is an underestimate. The 2030 figure is a projection with stated uncertainty, not a measurement. (The IEA's own pages could not be opened on 1 November 2026; check them, and its later Key questions on energy and AI, if you can.) On the device: some small models run on phones and laptops (for example Apple's roughly 3-billion-parameter model, 2024), while most large tools run in data centres. Taiwan's share of the most advanced chip-making (92%) is from a 2021 Semiconductor Industry Association study. Singapore paused new data centres in 2019; in 2021 they used about 7% of its electricity (Kontinentalist). The earlier draft's “30 to 50 long-term jobs” (Good Jobs First, via AP, scope not stated) and UNEP's “800 kg of materials for a 2 kg computer” (no source given) were removed. The fish farmer in the AP story worried about longer power cuts, like Hana.

educatorNotes.1.source: Rules for data centres in Johor and Batam change quickly (in early 2026, after residents protested about water, Malaysia stopped new applications for non-AI data centres in Johor and tightened water approvals, Kontinentalist reports). Check the latest news before teaching the third section. Data centres also run websites, videos and messages, not only AI. Benefits are real too: investment (AP reports over US$31 billion for Malaysia in the first 10 months of 2024, from Knight Frank), building work and some long-term jobs; UNEP also notes that AI can help to monitor the environment. Some places give data centres large tax breaks, so ask who gains from a deal.
